newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-U.S. Jews and Israel -- a house divided.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-U.S. Jews and Israel -- a house divided.

text.p: In Bill Clinton, Israel has never had a stronger ally in the White House.

Yet behind the perceived power of the Jewish lobby in Washington stands an American Jewish community that is split over Middle East peace policy and increasingly absorbed with its own problems of survival.
The battles between Israel's Likud-led government and opposition Labour party have spilled over to the United States, Jewish community leaders and lobbyists say.

Some fear the infighting could weaken the lobby's influence and widen the divide among America's 5.5 million Jews, most of whom are liberal and will vote for Clinton and his Democratic party in Tuesday's elections, polls show.

Jewish leaders acknowledge that the Jewish lobby never presents a completely unified front unless Israel's security is threatened. But since Israel's ousted Labour government signed the 1993 Oslo accords on Palestinian self-rule the rift has widened, they say.

"I think it's truer now than it's ever been," said Dob Zakheim, a former Pentagon official. "The battles that should be fought in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem are now being fought not only in New York but in the halls of Congress. This has a deleterious effect on the U.S.-Israel relationship," Zakheim said.
Lobbyists who backed peacemaking by Labour leaders Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres resented attempts by Likud supporters to lobby Congress.

"Most of the Jewish community in America approved of President Clinton's obvious support for what Rabin was doing," said a senior official of one Jewish-American group. "It was unthinkable that some groups would lobby against that on Capitol Hill. They crossed the red line," said the official, who asked not to be identified.
"I think that was wrong," said Phil Baum, executive director of the non-partisan World Jewish Congress. "We are trying to avoid the game that we know better than the Israelis," he said.
It is hardly surprising that American Jews should differ on Oslo when the issue split Israeli society right down the middle and led to Rabin's assassination.

"For us there used to be one issue -- 'Security, Stupid'," said one Jewish leader. "After Oslo it became more complex and Rabin urged us to adjust, he didn't want to be told by American Jews how to run Israel," the leader, who asked not to be identified, said.

Rabin's death and the ousting of his successor Shimon Peres by Likud's Benjamin Netanyahu in May elections rattled the Clinton administration, which openly backed Peres, and sharpened the strategy debate within U.S. Jewry.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) denies that American Jews are seriously split.
"The community is more united than ever," said Howard Kohr, AIPAC's executive director.
But battle lines for a second-term Clinton administration are already drawn should the president decide to forge ahead with Oslo.
"Likud gets support on the Hill, Labour among the administration," Zakheim said.

"In Congress Netanyahu has a brake on any really international move to pressure him. He is not strong enough to get Congress to dictate foreign policy to Clinton...but he can have a negative rather than positive influence," Zakheim said.

Political pundits are divided on whether Clinton will "get tough" on Netanyahu during a second term. But they agree that unless Israel's survival is at stake, American Jews will increasingly focus on their own problems.
"Continuity is the one issue on people's minds," said Jonathan Mahler, an editor of the Jewish weekly Forward.
American Jews are assimilating into secular American society and marrying non-Jews at a rate that alarms community leaders.
"The intermarriage rate is 50 percent," says Baum.
The Jewish population has not grown in two generations while other ethnic minorities such as Asians, Hispanics and African-Americans have mushroomed.
This will eventually translate into a loss of voting muscle.
"The Jewish vote is declining proportionally and dispersing," Baum said. "It could have an adverse effect on Jewish political strength."

The Jewish vote is concentrated in several key states and Jewish political and financial support for candidates is still important. The current Congress counts 10 Jews in the Senate and 25 in the House.
But population dispersal, the redrawing of congressional districts and possible reform of election campaign funding are potential political worries, Jewish leaders say.
"As the Jewish community self-destructs through assimilation and intermarriage, so it weakens," Zakheim says.
American Jews are as concerned that such weakness lessens their influence over general domestic political issues, Jewish schooling, church-state relations and abortion as they are about Israel.
"American Jews are relatively apathetic towards the Middle East," Zakheim said. "Only 20 percent of American Jews have visited Israel...Few speak Hebrew."
Leaders like Baum have seen the writing on the wall. "Jews will rally if Israel is in crisis," he says, but adds: "The Jewish community is going to have to husband its strength better.
"We are barely holding our own."
